Abstract This study evaluated how sustainable entrepreneurship and various dynamic capabilities have affected the livelihood of family-based handicraft businesses, especially the "Moonj craft and Pattal(Leaf plate)" in India. This is a sustainable and traditional business where women or family members carry out maximum business and economic activity in India's handmade Moonj craft and Pattal industry. The research used an online poll of 410 family members working for female-owned Indian handicraft businesses such as Moonj Craft, Pattal making, and traditional cot making in India. PLS- SEM for factor loading and SPSS-26, a statistical software, have been used for data analysis to determine how pandemic and sustainable entrepreneurship affect India's family-based handicraft business (Moonj Craft). The model demonstrated that independent constructs such as Sustainable entrepreneurship and other factors significantly influence the livelihood of the family-based craft industry, particularly Moonj art, in some states of India. The advancement of digital technology, social media, and AI use for marketing handmade products has increased the productivity and attraction of female artisans to start new businesses for sustainable development. Because of these issues, sustainable entrepreneurship, has become increasingly important. Sustainable entrepreneurial technology is essential in transforming toward a more flexible eco- friendly environment and future greening and thus has a vital role in connecting economic, social, and ecological aims. This study explores the impact of sustainable entrepreneurship on the Moonj craft and Pattal industry, as this product is entirely sustainable, naturally obtained, and easily degradable. Thus, this research focuses on how Sustainable entrepreneurship using digital social media after the pandemic has affected family-based businesses such as Moonj Craft, women's roles and concerns in the craft sector. This study also suggested some innovative strategies for developing a family-based craft industry. It will also help academicians, policymakers, managers, and researchers explore their ideas globally in other family-based handicraft industries. JSON: Name: moonj_pattal_sustainable_entrepreneurship Title: Mixed‐methods quantitative analysis (PLS‐SEM and binary logistic regression) of the impact of sustainable entrepreneurship and digital capabilities on survival and household livelihoods in family‐based Moonj craft and Pattal enterprises in India Short Hypothesis: Higher adoption of sustainable entrepreneurship practices combined with greater digital capability (social media, digital payments, AI‐enabled marketing) increases the probability of firm survival and raises household income resilience among family‐based Moonj craft and Pattal enterprises after COVID‐19 lockdowns. Related Work: Existing work investigates sustainable entrepreneurship, dynamic capabilities, and digital adoption in SMEs and handicrafts using cross‐sectional surveys and structural equation models. Prior studies show correlations between digital tools (e‐commerce, social media), entrepreneurial leadership, and firm performance, and separate literature documents COVID‐19 shocks to small craft enterprises. Limitations of current approaches include heavy reliance on cross‐sectional self‐reported data, limited treatment of domain‐specific crafts (Moonj/pattal), inconsistent measurement of digital capability (often coarse binary indicators), scarce evaluation of AI or advanced digital tools, weak handling of endogeneity or causality, and little comparative testing against machine‐learning baselines. Generalizability is constrained by regionally focused samples and convenience sampling. There is also limited investigation of mediation (e.g., innovation, talent management) and few ablation studies isolating sustainable entrepreneurship from digital capability effects. Abstract: This research pipeline addresses whether sustainable entrepreneurship and digital capability jointly improve the survival and household livelihood resilience of family‐based Moonj craft and Pattal (leaf plate) enterprises in India following COVID‐19 disruptions. We propose a quantitative analysis combining PLS‐SEM to validate measurement constructs (sustainable entrepreneurship, digital capability, innovation, talent management) and binary logistic regression plus machine‐learning classifiers to predict firm survival and income resilience. Primary data comprise a structured survey of family artisans (target N≈410) supplemented by administrative MSME/ODOP records. Main contributions: (1) validated, domain‐adapted measurement model for sustainable entrepreneurship in handicrafts; (2) causal‐inference oriented evaluation of digital capability and sustainability effects on survival and income; (3) ablation and robustness comparisons across statistical and ML baselines. Expected outcomes include quantified effect sizes for policy levers (digital training, financing, AI marketing), validated mediators (innovation, talent management), and evidence to guide targeted support for female‐led family craft enterprises. Experiments: Datasets: Primary structured survey of family‐based Moonj/pattal artisans (target N=410; geographic strata: Uttar Pradesh districts Bhadohi, Gorakhpur, Prayagraj, Kumbh market areas, plus purposive samples from Bihar and Maharashtra); administrative registries (MSME, ODOP) for firm registration, pre‐ and post‐pandemic revenue where available; secondary socio‐demographic covariates from local census. Preprocessing: Missing‐value rules (drop if >20% missing), impute remaining numeric values with median per stratum, categorical encoding, standardize continuous predictors. Measurement model: PLS‐SEM with observed items grouped into constructs (sustainable entrepreneurship, digital capability: SM/DT/AI, entrepreneurial leadership, innovation, talent management); assess reliability (Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability), convergent validity (AVE), discriminant validity (HTMT). Structural model: bootstrap (5,000 resamples) for path coefficients and mediation tests. Primary outcome models: (A) Binary survival model (survived vs. ceased operations after lockdown) estimated with logistic regression (cluster‐robust SE by village/tehsil) and compared with Random Forest and XGBoost classifiers; (B) Continuous outcome model for change in monthly household income (post minus pre lockdown) using OLS and Random Forest regression. Baselines: (1) model without sustainable entrepreneurship variables; (2) model without digital capability variables; (3) standard logistic/OLS only; (4) ML models with full features. Evaluation metrics: For classification — accuracy, AUC‐ROC, precision, recall, F1, calibration (Hosmer‐Lemeshow and Generalized HL); for regression — R^2, RMSE, MAE, and standardized beta coefficients. Experimental protocol: 70/30 stratified train/test split by district; 5‐fold cross‐validation on training set for hyperparameter tuning of ML models; report test set metrics and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals for coefficients and feature importances. Ablation studies: remove (a) digital capability features, (b) sustainable entrepreneurship features, (c) AI‐related item only, (d) innovation and talent management mediators; compare change in AUC/R^2 and path coefficients. Robustness checks: propensity score matching on observable confounders for treatment defined as high sustainable entrepreneurship score; instrumental variable sensitivity analysis if plausible instruments (e.g., distance to ODOP centre) available. Risk Factors and Limitations: Self‐report bias and recall error in survey measures (pre/post income); survivorship and selection bias (companies that ceased may be underreported); sampling bias from mixed random/convenience sampling and regional focus limits external validity beyond studied districts and crafts; cross‐sectional design limits causal identification and raises endogeneity risk (reverse causality and omitted variables) despite PSM/IV robustness checks; measurement validity risk for novel constructs (AI capability) with limited prior scales; cluster correlation and small cluster counts may inflate Type I error if not adjusted; limited sample size for complex ML models—risk of overfitting and unstable feature importance; administrative records may be incomplete or non‐standardized; heterogeneity across subregions and product types may limit generalization to other handicraft sectors; computational demands modest but repeated bootstrap/ML tuning increases runtime; ethical risks include privacy of artisan income and consent management.
